771.event_title: Darius I carves the Behistun relief over his defeated rivals
771.event: After winning the Persian throne, Darius I had a great relief and inscription carved high on the cliff at Bisotun, beside the ancient road from Mesopotamia to the Iranian plateau. The relief shows Darius, holding a bow as a sign of sovereignty, with his foot on a figure identified as the usurper Gaumata, and a line of bound captives standing before him. The text, in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian, records how he overthrew Gaumata, defeated the rebels who claimed the kingdom, and took the throne.
771.explanation: The monument turned the defeat of a king's opponents into a permanent warning in stone for everyone who travelled the road.
771.tie_back: The kural's warrior warns enemies not to stand against his lord, since many who did now stand as stones, and at Behistun those who rose against Darius stand forever carved in stone before him.
771._accuracy_note: A partial fit: the stone images are of defeated rivals rather than Tamil hero-stones for the fallen, and it is the king's own boast rather than a soldier's.

772.event_title: Porus fights Alexander at the Hydaspes and keeps his kingdom
772.event: When Alexander the Great invaded the Punjab, Ambhi, the king of Taxila, submitted, but Porus, who ruled the land between the Hydaspes and Acesines rivers, chose to resist. At the Battle of the Hydaspes his elephants and infantry were outmatched by Alexander's mobile cavalry and mounted archers, and he was defeated. Impressed by his skill and spirit, Alexander allowed Porus to keep his kingdom and may have given him further territory.
772.explanation: Porus took on the most formidable army of his age and lost, yet his choice to fight earned him a respect that his neighbour's easy submission did not.
772.tie_back: The kural says it is better to hold a spear that missed an elephant than an arrow that killed a hare, and Porus, who aimed at the mightiest foe and failed, ended with more honour than one who bowed without a fight.
772._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of honour won by attempting the greatest opponent, with the added apt detail of Porus's own war elephants.

773.event_title: The captain of the Admiral Hipper rescues Glowworm's crew and praises her commander
773.place: Norwegian Sea, off the coast of Norway
773.event: The British destroyer HMS Glowworm, under Lieutenant Commander Gerard Roope, met the much larger German heavy cruiser Admiral Hipper, engaged her and rammed her before Glowworm sank. Hipper's captain, Hellmuth Heye, stopped for over an hour to pick up survivors from the sea. He later sent word to the British through the Red Cross praising Roope's courage in closing with a far stronger ship, and Roope was posthumously awarded the Victoria Cross, gazetted in 1945.
773.explanation: In the midst of a battle he had just won, an enemy commander used his ship to save his opponents and then made sure their captain's bravery would be honoured.
773.tie_back: The kural calls fearlessness valour but says helping the enemy when misfortune strikes him is its sharp edge, and Captain Heye's rescue of Glowworm's crew is that edge in action.
773._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of the kural: a victor aiding a defeated enemy in distress and honouring his courage.

774.event_title: Rifleman Lachhiman Gurung fights on one-handed at Taungdaw
774.place: Taungdaw, west bank of the Irrawaddy, Burma (Myanmar)
774.event: Rifleman Lachhiman Gurung of the 4th Battalion, 8th Gurkha Rifles, was manning the most forward post of his platoon when it was attacked by a large enemy force at night. He threw back two grenades that landed in his trench, but a third exploded in his right hand, severely wounding him. Alone and disregarding his wounds, he loaded and fired his rifle with his left hand for about four hours, and his example helped his comrades hold their position; he was awarded the Victoria Cross, gazetted in July 1945.
774.explanation: Badly wounded and with his weapon hand gone, he simply carried on fighting with what he had left.
774.tie_back: The kural's hero, having thrown his only spear, finds another in his own wound and smiles, and Lachhiman Gurung, his hand shattered, turned at once to fighting on with the other.
774._accuracy_note: A strong match for undiminished fighting spirit after a grievous wound, though there is no record of laughter.

775.event_title: Theodore Roosevelt delivers his speech after being shot
775.event: While campaigning for president as the Progressive Party candidate, Theodore Roosevelt was shot in the chest by a would-be assassin as he left his hotel in Milwaukee. The bullet passed through his folded speech manuscript and metal glasses case and lodged near his ribs. Refusing to go to hospital first, Roosevelt went on to the auditorium and spoke for about an hour, showing the audience the bullet-pierced manuscript, before he accepted medical treatment.
775.explanation: Roosevelt treated the attack as no reason to flinch from what he had come to do, and the bullet remained in his body for the rest of his life.
775.tie_back: The kural says that for the truly brave even a blink in the face of the enemy's spear counts as retreat, and Roosevelt would not let a bullet make him turn from his audience.
775._accuracy_note: A reasonable illustration of refusing to show fear, though it is a political speech rather than battle and comes after the blow rather than before it.

776.event_title: Adrian Carton de Wiart returns to the front again and again
776.place: Somaliland and the Western Front (France and Belgium)
776.event: Adrian Carton de Wiart, a British Army officer, lost an eye in Somaliland early in the First World War and later lost his left hand on the Western Front. He kept returning to active service and was wounded many times in that war, by one count eight times. In July 1916 he was awarded the Victoria Cross for his leadership of the 8th Battalion, Gloucestershire Regiment, at La Boisselle during the Battle of the Somme.
776.explanation: Rather than treating each wound as a reason to step back, he treated it as an interruption before returning to the fighting.
776.tie_back: The kural's hero counts as wasted every day without an honourable wound, and Carton de Wiart's repeated return to the front shows a man who measured his days by service under fire.
776._accuracy_note: A strong portrait of the warrior who welcomes wounds, though the sources do not record him counting days in this way.

777.event_title: Queen Victoria institutes the Victoria Cross for valour
777.event: A royal warrant of 29 January 1856 created the Victoria Cross as Britain's highest award for gallantry in the face of the enemy, backdated to cover acts in the Crimean War. Unlike earlier honours, it was open to all ranks. At the first investiture, in Hyde Park on 26 June 1857, Queen Victoria personally presented the cross to 62 recipients before large crowds.
777.explanation: The decoration was deliberately reserved for proven courage rather than rank or birth, so that wearing it meant one had risked one's life.
777.tie_back: The kural says the warrior's anklet is a true ornament only on those who seek lasting fame and do not cling to life, and the Victoria Cross was designed as just such a badge, fitting only on those whose valour is real.
777._accuracy_note: A reasonable modern parallel to the heroic anklet, but it is the founding of an award rather than a deed of valour.

778.event_title: No. 303 Polish Squadron's first victory while still held back from combat
778.place: RAF Northolt and the skies over Hertfordshire, England, United Kingdom
778.event: No. 303 Squadron, formed of Polish airmen at RAF Northolt in August 1940, had not yet been declared operational and was flying a training exercise when Pilot Officer Ludwik Paszkiewicz saw enemy aircraft, broke formation and shot down a German Messerschmitt Bf 110. On landing he was reprimanded by his British commander for indiscipline and then congratulated for his success. The squadron was declared operational the next day and became the most successful Fighter Command unit in the Battle of Britain.
778.explanation: Kept out of the fight by those in authority, the Polish pilots lost none of their eagerness to defend the country that had taken them in.
778.tie_back: The kural says warriors who do not fear for their lives keep their fervour even when their king holds them back, and the Polish airmen's zeal survived both official doubt and a reprimand.
778._accuracy_note: A good fit for zeal surviving a commander's restraint; the restraint was a training status and a rebuke rather than royal anger.

779.event_title: Leonidas and his Spartans remain at Thermopylae
779.event: When a Persian force found a mountain path around the Greek position at the pass of Thermopylae, most of the allied Greek army left. The Spartan king Leonidas and his 300 Spartans stayed to hold the pass, together with contingents including some 700 Thespians, and were killed. Herodotus, the main source, reports that Leonidas thought it unfitting for the Spartans to desert the post they had been sent to hold, though he presents some details as hearsay.
779.explanation: Thermopylae was a military defeat, yet the defenders who died holding their post became one of history's lasting symbols of honour.
779.tie_back: The kural asks who could blame those who die keeping the vow they made, and no one has ever reproached Leonidas's men for losing a battle they died to keep faith with.
779._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of death in fidelity to duty placing defenders beyond blame; the exact reasons for staying are debated by historians.

780.event_title: Lincoln weeps for Colonel Elmer Ellsworth
780.place: Alexandria, Virginia, and the White House, Washington, D.C., United States
780.event: Colonel Elmer Ellsworth, a young officer and close friend of President Abraham Lincoln, was shot and killed in Alexandria, Virginia, after removing a Confederate flag from the roof of the Marshall House inn, becoming one of the first Union officers to die in the Civil War. Lincoln wept at the news. At his order Ellsworth's body lay in state in the East Room of the White House, where both the President and Mary Lincoln wept during the funeral.
780.explanation: The death of one young officer moved the nation's leader to open grief and made Ellsworth a national symbol in the war's first weeks.
780.tie_back: The kural says a warrior's death is worth begging for if it brings tears to the eyes of the leader who cared for him, and Ellsworth's death drew exactly such tears from Lincoln.
780._accuracy_note: A close match to the kural's image of a leader's tears for a fallen soldier he had cherished.
